newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels extend their grip in eastern Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels extend their grip in eastern Zaire.

text.p: Zairean rebels are extending their grip on eastern Zaire and say their next target is the river port of Kisangani in the diamond-hunters' haven of Upper Zaire region.
Zairean refugees who fled to Uganda and Ugandan military sources said rebels captured the town of Bunia in northeastern Zaire on Monday night, routing Zairean troops on the rampage.
Earlier on Tuesday the rebels said they had seized Bunia and Walikale to the west but there was no confirmation of the fall of Walikale as panicked foreigners pulled out of the northeast.

The rebellion broke out in October among Zaireans of Rwandan origin whom the government threatened to repatriate, along with more than a million Rwandan Hutu refugees who took refuge in Zaire after the genocide of Tutsis and moderate Hutus in 1994.
The fighting has scattered hundreds of thousands of Rwandan refugees and displaced Zaireans deep into the countryside.

Zairean rebel officer Jean Kabongo said on Tuesday the rebel Alliance of Democratic Forces had captured parts of Kisangani, the biggest city in the region. Aid agencies reported it was still in government hands.
"There will be a big combat for Kisangani but our forces have been there, around it, for a month," he told Reuters in the eastern Zairean city of Goma, which borders on western Rwanda.
In the past few years diamonds have given a new lease of life to Kisangani, which has been hit by a wave of looting by Zairean soldiers who have fled rebel advances since October.

The rebels have not said they are after diamonds, but are likely to need significant funds both for armaments and to persuade starving, suddenly dislocated people in the region they occupy that they can do better than the previous rulers.
"Bunia has fallen to the Zairean rebels. That is our understanding of the situation," said a Ugandan military source on Tuesday in the Ugandan town of Kasese, 165 km (100 miles) to the south.
Zairean refugees among 3,000 who fled to Kasese said Zairean soldiers looted Bunia, beat up residents and raped many women before they left the town which fell to rebels on Monday night.

Bunia, 370 km (230 miles) north of the rebel capital Goma, is the northernmost town confirmed to have fallen into rebel hands. They now control towns across a front 550 km (340 miles) long from north to south, parallel with Zaire's eastern borders.
The turmoil in central Africa which threatens to spill out of eastern Zaire is overshadowing the 19th Franco-African summit opening on Wednesday in Ouagadougou, capital of Burkina Faso.

Rwanda and Uganda are virtually at war with Zaire and fighting is raging in Burundi between the Tutsi-dominated army and Hutu rebels. The Central African Republic is mired in its third army mutiny this year.
The Great Lakes conflict and long debate on a multinational force charged with helping refugees fleeing fighting have underlined France's waning role as the gendarme of Africa.
Canadian Raymond Chretien, the U.N. envoy trying to resolve the crisis in eastern Zaire, was expected to meet ailing Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko on Wednesday on the French Riviera.
Chretien, who arrived in France on Monday after touring African capitals, was staying at Menton near Mobutu's luxury villa overlooking the Mediterranean at Roquebrune-Cap-Martin.
"We are working on our final report" on the Zaire crisis, Chretien's spokesman Georges Riou said. Chretien is to report to U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali on December 11.

Ending a diplomatic tug-of-war between Paris and Kinshasa, an aide to Mobutu said on Tuesday Zaire would let France try its ambassador to Paris whose car hit two boys in Menton. One was killed instantly on November 23 and the other died on Saturday.
A Ugandan military source said rebels on Tuesday were clearing pockets of resistance in Bunia. Zaire's government accuses Ugandan troops of fighting alongside Tutsi rebels.
Some of the refugees who reached Kasese said they heard armed men speaking Ugandan languages inside Zaire but they could not tell whether they were regular Ugandan government troops.
Ugandan Army Commander Major-General Mugisha Muntu said Ugandan troops crossed only three km (two miles) into Zaire and "annihilated" Ugandan rebels based there before pulling back.
